AI for Management — Case Study
Task 1: Inventory & Initial Scan
1. Metadata Table
Automated extraction of metadata and content boundaries for the 28 documents in the Document Set. Snippets are factual descriptions of each paper's stated scope; no evaluative or cross-document conclusions are drawn at this stage.
2. Domain Boundary Definition
Scope of the knowledge domain
The Document Set covers the application of artificial intelligence and operations-research methods to operational complexity reduction, energy efficiency, and intelligent automation in energy-intensive industrial production — predominantly steel and metal manufacturing (reheating/heat-treatment furnaces, hot/cold rolling, steelmaking–continuous casting, forging). The scope spans both the optimization problem (how to schedule jobs, furnaces, and energy flows) and the AI/decision-support layer (how such optimization is learned, explained, or trusted by human operators).
Main sub-domains / clusters identified
Energy-efficient / green scheduling for furnaces and flow shops — classical and metaheuristic optimization (MILP, genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, PSO, grey wolf optimization, matheuristics, migrating-birds optimization) applied to reheating, heat-treatment, and hybrid flow-shop scheduling (Docs 1, 2, 3, 7, 12, 14, 15, 19, 20, 24, 26, 28).
Deep Reinforcement Learning for scheduling and energy management — DRL, multi-agent RL, and LLM-assisted RL applied to steel-plant energy dispatch, demand response, and job-shop/production scheduling (Docs 5, 9, 13, 17, 18).
Digital Twins — virtual-physical integration for real-time monitoring, prediction, and scheduling of furnaces and rolling processes (Docs 10, 16, 23, 27).
Explainable AI (XAI) and human-AI collaboration — techniques (SHAP, counterfactual explanations, decision-tree surrogates) and conceptual frameworks (intelligence augmentation, human-in/on-the-loop) for making AI-driven scheduling and process-safety decisions transparent and trustworthy (Docs 4, 6, 8, 13, 22).
Multi-agent / service-oriented systems — decentralized coordination for product reallocation, demand response, and service-based production planning (Docs 9, 11, 18, 27).
Uncertainty-aware scheduling — forecasting-based and robust/stochastic optimization for gas supply, release times, and processing-time uncertainty (Docs 3, 5, 21, 25).
Analyst tools and techniques applied in this task
This inventory was produced using automated PDF metadata and abstract extraction (via pdftotext) to determine title, authorship, source, and publication data, cross-referenced with in-text keyword blocks where present, and manual classification of each abstract into candidate thematic clusters. This inventory forms the basis for Task 2 (Topographical Mapping), where these clusters will be formalized into a hierarchical topic tree and cross-reference network.
AI for Management — Case Study
Task 2: Thematic Analysis & Knowledge Structure Mapping
Document Set: 28 papers (see Task 1: Inventory & Initial Scan)
This report builds on the Task 1 inventory to organize the Document Set into thematic clusters, map recurring concepts and their relationships, and present a comparative methodology table across all 28 papers. Papers are identified by author(s) and year; a numbered Paper Index (Table 0) is provided below for cross-reference with the tables and figures that follow.
Table 0 — Paper Index
1. Thematic Clusters
Six thematic clusters were identified across the Document Set based on each paper's primary research focus, method family, and application target. Several papers address more than one cluster; these are noted explicitly and are visualized as cross-cluster links in the Cross-Reference Network Graph (Section 5).
Cluster C1 — Energy-Efficient / Green Scheduling for Furnaces and Flow Shops
Papers: Benedikt et al. (2021); Wang, Liu & Jin (2019); Long et al. (2020); Wang et al. (2016); Han et al. (2020); Duan et al. (2025); Rao & Zhang (2025); Gomes et al. (2021); Xu et al. (2024); Sobottka et al. (2020); Liu et al. (2020); Hidri et al. (2021).
Central topic: Minimizing energy consumption (idle energy, gas/heating energy, or energy cost) and/or tardiness and makespan in furnace-centric and flow-shop production scheduling, using mathematical programming and metaheuristic search.
Key methods / technologies:
Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) for exact scheduling and dispatching formulations
Metaheuristics: genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, particle swarm optimization, grey wolf optimization, migrating birds optimization
Matheuristics combining MILP with variable neighborhood search
Fuzzy logic for representing uncertain processing times and due dates
GA-optimized neural network (GA-BP) for energy-consumption prediction
Deterministic online (real-time) scheduling algorithms
Cluster C2 — Deep Reinforcement Learning for Scheduling & Energy Management
Papers: Wang et al. (2025, IEEE TIE); Shah et al. (2026); Theumer et al. (2022); Zeng et al. (2025); Bashyal et al. (2025).
Central topic: Applying (multi-agent) deep reinforcement learning — in some cases combined with human feedback, large language models, or attention mechanisms — to learn scheduling and energy-dispatch policies for energy-intensive discrete manufacturing and demand response.
Key methods / technologies:
Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Deep-Q-Learning
Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) with centralized training / decentralized execution
Attention mechanisms for state representation under partial observability (POMDP)
LLM-assisted reward-function design via human feedback
Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks as policy function approximators
Cluster C3 — Digital Twins for Production Monitoring & Scheduling
Papers: Li et al. (2026, IEEE TII); Li et al. (2024, ESWA); Liu et al. (2019); Müller-Zhang et al. (2023).
Central topic: Constructing virtual representations (digital twins) of physical production assets — reheating furnaces, rolling mills — synchronized with real-time data to improve scheduling accuracy, parameter prediction, and live decision-making.
Key methods / technologies:
Five-dimension digital twin architectures (physical entity, virtual entity, data space, services, connections)
IoT-based data integration across upstream/downstream production lines
Gradient boosting (LightGBM) and population-based algorithms for parameter prediction
NSGA-II / modified simulated-annealing-PSO hybrids (SA-MOPSO) for multi-objective scheduling
Deep-Q-Learning integrated with digital twin feedback loops
Cluster C4 — Explainable AI (XAI) & Human-AI Collaboration
Papers: Wang & Chen (2024); Morandini et al. (2023); Mehdiyev et al. (2024); Theumer et al. (2022); Arunthavanathan et al. (2024).
Central topic: Making AI-driven scheduling, production-control, or process-safety decisions interpretable and trustworthy to human operators, through post-hoc explanation techniques or explicit human-in/on-the-loop design.
Key methods / technologies:
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME post-hoc explanation methods
Counterfactual explanation search (NSGA-II-based)
Decision-tree surrogate models and visualization techniques (contribution diagrams, improved bar charts)
Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA) applied to AI vs. intelligence-augmentation comparisons
Human-in-the-loop / human-on-the-loop / AI-in-the-loop taxonomies
Cluster C5 — Multi-Agent & Service-Oriented Systems
Papers: Neuer et al. (2016); Theumer et al. (2022); Bashyal et al. (2025).
Central topic: Decentralized coordination among autonomous agents (representing products, orders, or machines) to reallocate, schedule, or negotiate resources, often through service-oriented architectures or auction mechanisms.
Key methods / technologies:
Holonic multi-agent systems (MAS)
Service-oriented architecture (SOA) and semantic modelling / ontologies
Virtual marketplace and auction-based pricing mechanisms
Multi-agent reinforcement learning with cooperative reward structures
Cluster C6 — Uncertainty-Aware / Robust Scheduling
Papers: Long et al. (2020); Wang et al. (2025, IEEE TIE); Pena et al. (2019); Zhang et al. (2023).
Central topic: Handling stochastic or forecast-based uncertainty — release times, gas flows, processing times, energy prices — in production scheduling through robust optimization, chance-constrained programming, or rolling-horizon re-planning.
Key methods / technologies:
Robust optimization (RO) and equivalent mixed-integer linear reformulations
Chance-constrained programming (CCP) with Monte Carlo simulation
Time-series forecasting (Holt-Winters, ARIMA-type models)
Benders’ decomposition for exact solution of robust scheduling models
Rolling-horizon MILP re-optimization
2. Recurring Concepts & Terminology
Ten recurring concepts were identified across the Document Set. Each concept links methods, application areas, and the overarching themes of operational complexity reduction, energy efficiency, and intelligent automation.
2.1 Concept-to-Paper Mapping
2.2 Concept Relationships (Summary)
The ten concepts above are not independent: they connect through shared papers and shared application areas. In general terms:
Energy Efficiency is the most frequent cross-cutting objective; it is pursued either directly through mathematical/metaheuristic scheduling (Mathematical Programming, Metaheuristics) or indirectly through learning-based control (Deep Reinforcement Learning).
Production/Job Scheduling is the common problem structure underlying nearly all clusters — it is the task to which Mathematical Programming, Metaheuristics, Deep Reinforcement Learning, and Multi-Agent Systems are each applied as a solution method.
Digital Twin and Multi-Agent Systems represent two distinct system-architecture approaches (centralized virtual model vs. decentralized agent coordination) for the same underlying goal of real-time, adaptive scheduling.
Explainable AI (XAI) is applied downstream of Metaheuristics, Deep Reinforcement Learning, or general AI-based decision systems, rather than being a scheduling method in itself — it addresses the interpretability of decisions already produced by those methods.
Uncertainty / Robust Optimization and Prediction / Surrogate Modelling frequently co-occur, since forecasting models (e.g., release-time or energy-price prediction) are commonly the mechanism by which uncertainty is characterized before a robust or chance-constrained schedule is generated.
A fully hierarchical representation of these relationships is provided in Section 4 (Hierarchical Topic Tree).

AI for Management — Case Study
Task 3: Cross-Paper Synthesis & Research Insights
Building on Task 1 (Inventory) and Task 2 (Thematic Analysis & Knowledge Structure Mapping)
This report synthesizes findings across the 28 papers in the Document Set, organized by the six thematic clusters established in Task 2 (C1–C6). For each cluster, the primary research focus, common methods, key operational problems, shared problem-solving approaches, and points of convergence/divergence are summarized. A cross-theme comparison and set of emerging trends follow, closing with an integrative synthesis narrative.
1. Theme-by-Theme Synthesis
C1 — Energy-Efficient / Green Scheduling for Furnaces and Flow Shops
Primary research focus: Minimizing energy consumption (idle energy, gas/heating energy, or energy cost) jointly with traditional scheduling objectives (makespan, tardiness) in furnace-centric and flow-shop production environments, predominantly in steel and metal manufacturing.
Common methods, models, technologies: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (Han et al., 2020; Gomes et al., 2021; Hidri et al., 2021); metaheuristics including genetic algorithms and simulated annealing (Sobottka et al., 2020; Hidri et al., 2021), particle swarm optimization, and migrating birds optimization (Han et al., 2020); grey wolf optimization (Rao & Zhang, 2025); fuzzy logic (Wang et al., 2016); matheuristics combining MILP with variable neighborhood search (Gomes et al., 2021); deterministic online algorithms (Xu et al., 2024); and a genetic-algorithm-optimized neural network for energy-consumption prediction (Duan et al., 2025).
Key operational or business problems addressed: Reducing idle-period energy waste in furnaces (Benedikt et al., 2021); coordinating interdependent sub-systems such as production scheduling and ladle dispatching (Han et al., 2020); balancing energy cost against tardiness penalties (Wang et al., 2016; Gomes et al., 2021); accounting for slab/billet deterioration during heating (Xu et al., 2024); accommodating mixed continuous/intermittent processing in forging (Liu et al., 2020); and eliminating idle-machine time across parallel machines (Hidri et al., 2021).
How papers approach similar challenges: Most papers formulate the problem as an exact optimization model (MILP or a fuzzy/robust variant) and then apply a metaheuristic or matheuristic to handle NP-hard, larger instances. Several papers treat energy and a traditional performance metric as a joint bi- or multi-objective problem (Wang et al., 2016; Gomes et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020), while others treat energy minimization as the dominant or sole objective (Benedikt et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2024; Rao & Zhang, 2025).
Convergence and divergence: Convergence: nearly all papers target furnace- or flow-shop-level scheduling in steel/metal production and rely on an “exact model + metaheuristic solver” pattern. Divergence: energy is represented in different ways — as a continuous function of machine dynamics (Benedikt et al., 2021), a deterioration-adjusted heating time (Xu et al., 2024), a fuzzy quantity under uncertainty (Wang et al., 2016), or a directly predicted neural-network output rather than an optimization variable (Duan et al., 2025). Solution techniques range from purely analytical (Benedikt et al., 2021) to purely metaheuristic (Rao & Zhang, 2025), with matheuristics (Gomes et al., 2021) in between.
C2 — Deep Reinforcement Learning for Scheduling & Energy Management
Primary research focus: Using deep reinforcement learning — increasingly combined with attention mechanisms, multi-agent coordination, or large language models — to learn scheduling and energy-dispatch policies rather than relying on an explicit mathematical model solved at runtime.
Common methods, models, technologies: Soft Actor-Critic (Wang et al., 2025); Proximal Policy Optimization (Shah et al., 2026; Theumer et al., 2022); Deep-Q-Learning; Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) formulations (Shah et al., 2026; Bashyal et al., 2025); attention mechanisms for state representation (Shah et al., 2026; Bashyal et al., 2025); multi-agent reinforcement learning with centralized-training/decentralized-execution (Bashyal et al., 2025; Theumer et al., 2022); and large-language-model-assisted reward design (Zeng et al., 2025).
Key operational or business problems addressed: Minimizing electricity cost under time-varying prices and renewable-generation uncertainty (Shah et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025); balancing production efficiency against energy cost in demand-response programs (Bashyal et al., 2025); reducing the manual effort of reward-function design and improving state representation for job-shop scheduling (Zeng et al., 2025); and maximizing logistic performance (lead time, inventory) in general production control (Theumer et al., 2022).
How papers approach similar challenges: All five papers frame the problem as a sequential decision process (MDP or POMDP), train a policy offline via simulation, and deploy it for fast online decisions — explicitly contrasted against MILP or rule-based approaches described as too slow for real-time deployment (Shah et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025). Several papers benchmark their DRL approach directly against a MILP baseline (Shah et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025).
Convergence and divergence: Convergence: a shared “offline training + online execution” pattern, and a consistent claim that DRL substantially reduces online computation time relative to re-solving MILP (Shah et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025). Divergence: coordination is single-agent (Shah et al., 2026) in some papers and multi-agent (Bashyal et al., 2025; Theumer et al., 2022) in others; uncertainty is explicitly modeled via a POMDP in some (Shah et al., 2026; Bashyal et al., 2025) and implicitly handled through a two-stage MDP design in another (Wang et al., 2025); and only one paper incorporates a large language model into the design process (Zeng et al., 2025).
C3 — Digital Twins for Production Monitoring & Scheduling
Primary research focus: Constructing a virtual, data-synchronized representation of a physical production asset (furnace, rolling mill) to improve the accuracy of scheduling decisions, parameter prediction, and real-time responsiveness.
Common methods, models, technologies: Five-dimension digital twin architectures — physical entity, virtual entity, data space, services, connections (Li et al., 2026); IoT-based data integration across production stages (Li et al., 2024); machine-learning prediction embedded in the twin, such as an improved LightGBM (Li et al., 2024) or a twin combined with NSGA-II and a modified SA-MOPSO (Liu et al., 2019); and Deep-Q-Learning integrated with the twin’s live data feed (Müller-Zhang et al., 2023).
Key operational or business problems addressed: Obtaining accurate charging/discharging times and real-time slab positions for reheating-furnace scheduling (Li et al., 2026); breaking down “information silos” between upstream and downstream rolling processes to improve dimensional accuracy (Li et al., 2024); enabling scheduling models to adapt dynamically as production conditions change (Liu et al., 2019); and supporting live, integrated process planning and scheduling for configurable, service-based production lines (Müller-Zhang et al., 2023).
How papers approach similar challenges: All four papers position the digital twin as a bridge between a physical process and a decision-making algorithm, supplying accurate real-time state information that a downstream optimization or learning method consumes. Three of the four pair the twin with a distinct optimization/learning technique (NSGA-II/SA-MOPSO in Liu et al., 2019; tabu search in Li et al., 2026; Deep-Q-Learning in Müller-Zhang et al., 2023), while Li et al. (2024) uses the twin mainly as a unified data platform feeding a prediction model.
Convergence and divergence: Convergence: all four report closed-loop or near-real-time operation (measurement → twin update → decision → execution) and all target steel/metal rolling or reheating processes. Divergence: the twins differ in formal “dimensionality” — Li et al. (2026) explicitly follows a published five-dimension DT framework, while Liu et al. (2019) and Müller-Zhang et al. (2023) describe twin-like architectures without adopting that specific formalism; the paired decision method also varies from evolutionary multi-objective optimization to reinforcement learning.
C4 — Explainable AI (XAI) & Human-AI Collaboration
Primary research focus: Making AI-driven scheduling, production-control, or process-safety decisions interpretable and trustworthy to the human operators who must act on or override them.
Common methods, models, technologies: SHAP (Theumer et al., 2022); counterfactual explanations generated via NSGA-II (Mehdiyev et al., 2024); decision-tree-based interpretation and visualization techniques such as contribution diagrams and improved bar charts (Wang & Chen, 2024); a structured literature review of XAI methods and metrics (Morandini et al., 2023); and a Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA)-based comparison of automated AI versus “intelligence augmentation” (Arunthavanathan et al., 2024).
Key operational or business problems addressed: Explaining genetic-algorithm-based scheduling outputs to factory workers who lack AI background knowledge (Wang & Chen, 2024); providing actionable “what-if” guidance for improving a job-shop schedule (Mehdiyev et al., 2024); identifying which XAI techniques and metrics are appropriate for planning and scheduling tools generally (Morandini et al., 2023); building operator trust in a multi-agent production-control system (Theumer et al., 2022); and determining which safety-critical decisions should remain with humans versus be delegated to AI (Arunthavanathan et al., 2024).
How papers approach similar challenges: The cluster divides into two approaches: post-hoc explanation of an already-produced model output (SHAP in Theumer et al., 2022; counterfactuals in Mehdiyev et al., 2024; decision-tree surrogates in Wang & Chen, 2024), and conceptual or taxonomic framing of where AI and humans should each contribute to a decision (Arunthavanathan et al., 2024; at a review level, Morandini et al., 2023).
Convergence and divergence: Convergence: all five papers treat interpretability as instrumental to trust and adoption, with several noting that a lack of transparency limits the practical acceptance of AI-based scheduling or control systems (Wang & Chen, 2024; Morandini et al., 2023). Divergence: three papers focus specifically on job/production scheduling explainability (Wang & Chen, 2024; Mehdiyev et al., 2024; Theumer et al., 2022), while Morandini et al. (2023) and Arunthavanathan et al. (2024) address a broader process-industry or process-safety context; the underlying AI system being explained also differs — GA output, MILP/ML-based schedules, and MARL policies, respectively.
C5 — Multi-Agent & Service-Oriented Systems
Primary research focus: Coordinating multiple autonomous agents — representing products, orders, machines, or facilities — to jointly reach scheduling, reallocation, or energy-management decisions without central, monolithic control.
Common methods, models, technologies: Holonic multi-agent systems and service-oriented architecture (SOA) with semantic modelling (Neuer et al., 2016); multi-agent reinforcement learning with cooperative, attention-based coordination (Bashyal et al., 2025); and multi-agent DRL (PPO) combined with a hierarchical, role-based action space (Theumer et al., 2022).
Key operational or business problems addressed: Reallocating off-spec steel products to alternative customer orders via a virtual marketplace (Neuer et al., 2016); coordinating energy-consuming and energy-generating agents across a discrete manufacturing facility for demand response (Bashyal et al., 2025); and assigning production-control decisions to agent “roles” corresponding to real organizational roles such as machine operators or foremen (Theumer et al., 2022).
How papers approach similar challenges: All three papers decompose a system-wide decision into local agent-level decisions, using either an explicit market/auction mechanism (Neuer et al., 2016) or a shared, cooperative reward signal that aligns individual agent behavior with a global objective (Bashyal et al., 2025; Theumer et al., 2022).
Convergence and divergence: Convergence: each paper explicitly aims to avoid the limitations of centralized decision-making, whether due to a lack of cross-plant communication (Neuer et al., 2016) or the scalability challenges of a single monolithic controller (Bashyal et al., 2025; Theumer et al., 2022). Divergence: Neuer et al. (2016) uses a rule/market-based coordination mechanism with no learning component, whereas Bashyal et al. (2025) and Theumer et al. (2022) use learned (MARL) policies; the application domain also differs — product-order matching versus energy/production scheduling.
C6 — Uncertainty-Aware / Robust Scheduling
Primary research focus: Explicitly accounting for stochastic or forecast-based uncertainty in scheduling inputs — release times, gas flows, processing times, energy prices — rather than assuming deterministic data.
Common methods, models, technologies: Robust optimization with equivalent MILP reformulations (Zhang et al., 2023); chance-constrained programming combined with Monte Carlo simulation (Long et al., 2020); time-series forecasting such as Holt-Winters and ARIMA-type models (Pena et al., 2019; Long et al., 2020); Benders’ decomposition for exact solution of robust models (Zhang et al., 2023); rolling-horizon MILP re-optimization (Pena et al., 2019); and a two-stage offline-learning/online-correction DRL framework (Wang et al., 2025).
Key operational or business problems addressed: Producing a schedule that remains feasible and low-cost despite uncertain job release times in steelmaking-continuous casting (Long et al., 2020); balancing by-product gas generation and consumption despite forecast error (Pena et al., 2019); scheduling hot strip mill operations despite uncertain processing times while reducing reheating-related energy consumption (Zhang et al., 2023); and optimizing a steel enterprise’s energy system despite supply/demand uncertainty (Wang et al., 2025).
How papers approach similar challenges: Three of the four papers follow a two-stage “forecast, then optimize/correct” pattern, in which a forecasting model characterizes the uncertain input and a second-stage optimization or correction mechanism produces the operational decision (Long et al., 2020; Pena et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025). Zhang et al. (2023) instead encodes uncertainty directly into a robust optimization model without an explicit forecasting stage.
Convergence and divergence: Convergence: all four papers describe deterministic scheduling as inefficient or infeasible under real operating conditions and propose an explicit mechanism to re-plan or correct decisions as new information arrives. Divergence: robust optimization is conservative by design (Zhang et al., 2023), whereas chance-constrained and rolling-horizon approaches (Long et al., 2020; Pena et al., 2019) allow a tunable trade-off between robustness and cost; Wang et al. (2025) additionally situates its approach's behavior relative to established robust and stochastic optimization baselines.
2. Comparative Analysis Across Themes
Shared objectives across research streams: reducing operational cost (energy, tardiness, makespan) while maintaining production feasibility; enabling faster and more autonomous decision-making than manual or expert-based scheduling; and improving the accuracy or timeliness of the data underlying those decisions.
Differences in methodologies and implementation approaches: C1 and C6 rely primarily on mathematical programming, metaheuristics, and statistical forecasting, typically solved per scheduling cycle rather than continuously. C2 and part of C5 rely on learned policies (DRL/MARL) trained offline but executed online at low computational cost. C3 (Digital Twins) is architecturally distinct: its central contribution is data/state accuracy rather than a specific solution algorithm, and it is frequently paired with methods from C1, C2, or C6 (e.g., NSGA-II in Liu et al., 2019; Deep-Q-Learning in Müller-Zhang et al., 2023). C4 (XAI) is methodologically distinct again, operating downstream of a decision already produced by another cluster's method rather than producing a decision itself.
Common AI techniques appearing across multiple domains: NSGA-II appears as a direct scheduling solver (C1: Wang et al., 2016), embedded within a digital twin (C3: Liu et al., 2019), and within an XAI counterfactual-search method (C4: Mehdiyev et al., 2024). SHAP and related post-hoc explanation methods (C4) are applied specifically to the outputs of a DRL/MARL policy (C2: Theumer et al., 2022), directly linking C2 and C4. MILP appears within C1 (direct scheduling), C4 (embedded in counterfactual search, Mehdiyev et al., 2024), and C6 (robust/rolling-horizon reformulations).
Relationships between operational complexity reduction, energy efficiency, and intelligent automation: Energy efficiency is most often pursued as an explicit optimization objective within C1 and C6 (Benedikt et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2016; Han et al., 2020; Gomes et al., 2021), while intelligent automation — in the sense of autonomous, learned, or self-adapting decision-making — is concentrated in C2, C3, and C5. Operational complexity reduction is addressed differently by each cluster: C1/C6 reduce complexity by decomposing a large scheduling problem into a tractable optimization model; C3 reduces complexity by providing a single accurate data source instead of siloed data; C5 reduces complexity by decomposing centralized decisions into decentralized agent-level decisions; and C4 addresses the complexity of understanding a decision, not just producing it.
Recurring architectural patterns: An “offline model + online decision” pattern recurs across C2 (policy trained offline, deployed online), C3 (twin continuously updated, decisions computed on demand), and C6 (forecast generated periodically, decision corrected online). A second recurring pattern is “exact/optimal model + metaheuristic for scale,” seen throughout C1 (Sobottka et al., 2020; Han et al., 2020; Gomes et al., 2021) and C6 (Zhang et al., 2023, combining Benders’ decomposition with a PSO heuristic).
3. Emerging Research Trends
Trend 1 — Increasing use of AI-driven optimization
Papers published from 2023 onward increasingly substitute or supplement mathematical-programming scheduling with learned policies (Shah et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2025; Bashyal et al., 2025), while earlier papers in the Document Set (2016–2021) rely predominantly on MILP and metaheuristics (Neuer et al., 2016; Han et al., 2020; Hidri et al., 2021).
Trend 2 — Integration of digital twins and cyber-physical systems
Four papers explicitly construct digital twins that synchronize physical and virtual production states (Liu et al., 2019; Li et al., 2024; Müller-Zhang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2026), each combining the twin with a downstream optimization or learning method rather than treating the twin as an end in itself.
Trend 3 — Growth of autonomous decision-making systems
Multiple papers explicitly compare their proposed method's online/real-time computational cost against traditional optimization, reporting that learned or twin-based approaches enable faster, more autonomous responses to disruptions than re-solving a mathematical program (Shah et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026).
Trend 4 — Convergence of scheduling, energy management, and automation functions
Several papers jointly optimize scheduling and energy objectives within a single automated framework rather than treating them as separate, sequential steps: Han et al. (2020) integrate production scheduling with ladle dispatching; Wang et al. (2025) and Bashyal et al. (2025) integrate scheduling with electricity- or demand-response management; and Zhang et al. (2023) link rolling-schedule decisions directly to reheat-energy reduction.
Trend 5 — Adoption of explainable or human-centered AI approaches

4. Synthesis Narrative
Across the 28 papers, the literature collectively addresses an organization's stated challenges — reducing operational complexity, improving energy efficiency, and deploying intelligent automation — through three largely complementary streams of work rather than a single unified methodology. The first stream (C1, C6) treats energy efficiency as an explicit optimization objective, most often paired with a traditional scheduling metric such as tardiness or makespan, and addresses operational complexity by formulating the problem exactly (MILP, robust optimization) and then applying a metaheuristic or matheuristic where exact solving does not scale. The second stream (C2, C3, C5) treats intelligent automation as the primary lens, using digital twins to supply accurate real-time state information, multi-agent systems to decompose centralized decisions, and deep reinforcement learning to replace repeated offline optimization with a fast, pre-trained online policy — several papers in this stream explicitly report that this shift reduces online computation time relative to MILP re-solving (Shah et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025). The third stream (C4) does not produce scheduling or energy decisions directly but instead addresses a problem that becomes more pressing as the other two streams grow more autonomous: ensuring that human operators can understand and, where necessary, override AI-generated decisions.
A recurring design principle across the Document Set is the separation of an offline or periodic modelling stage from an online or real-time decision stage — visible in the DRL “train offline, execute online” pattern (C2), the digital twin “continuously updated state, on-demand decision” pattern (C3), and the forecasting-based “forecast periodically, correct online” pattern (C6). This separation appears to be the literature's dominant response to the joint requirement for both optimization quality and real-time responsiveness. A second recurring principle is problem decomposition, whether by breaking a scheduling problem into a tractable mathematical model (C1), by breaking a centralized controller into cooperating agents (C5), or by breaking a monolithic “black-box” decision into locally interpretable components (C4).
Relationships between technologies, methods, and business objectives are consistent throughout: energy-efficiency objectives are most directly served by mathematical programming, metaheuristic, and robust-optimization methods (C1, C6); automation and responsiveness objectives are most directly served by digital twins, multi-agent systems, and reinforcement learning (C2, C3, C5); and the objective of maintaining human trust and oversight — which becomes more salient as the other two objectives are pursued more aggressively — is served by explainability methods (C4). The clusters are not fully independent: several papers (e.g., Wang et al., 2025; Theumer et al., 2022; Bashyal et al., 2025) combine methods from more than one stream, indicating that the literature is moving toward integrated frameworks that jointly address energy efficiency, automation, and interpretability rather than treating them as separate research problems.
AI for Management — Case Study
Task 4: Integrative Synthesis
A Unified Organizational Blueprint Integrating Digital Twins, Deep Reinforcement Learning, and Explainable AI
This report re-converges the diverged insights from Tasks 1–3 into a single, implementable organizational blueprint. It combines the strongest elements of each thematic cluster identified in Task 2 — energy-efficient/green scheduling (C1), Deep Reinforcement Learning (C2), Digital Twins (C3), Explainable AI (C4), Multi-Agent/Service-Oriented Systems (C5), and Uncertainty-Aware Scheduling (C6) — into a five-layer architecture, an operational workflow, a decision-governance model, and a phased deployment roadmap, while explicitly preserving the metallurgical and operational constraints identified across the Document Set.
1. Unified Architecture
The blueprint organizes the plant's technology stack into five layers, from the physical/metallurgical process at the base to human governance at the top. Digital Twins (C3) occupy the data layer, Deep Reinforcement Learning and optimization/metaheuristics (C1, C2, C6) occupy the decision layer, and Explainable AI (C4) forms a mandatory governance layer between AI-generated decisions and the humans who must act on them (see Figure 1, next page).
Layer descriptions
L1 — Physical & Metallurgical Process Layer: furnaces, ladles, rolling mills, and sensors/IoT devices. This layer encodes hard constraints that no upper layer may violate: minimum/maximum heating or residence time (Wang et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2024), FIFO and single-operation interlocks between charging, stepping, and extracting (Li et al., 2026), furnace/ladle capacity limits (Han et al., 2020), and deterioration effects on processing time (Xu et al., 2024; Wang, Liu & Jin, 2019).
L2 — Digital Twin Layer: a five-dimension digital twin — physical entity, virtual entity, data space, services, connections — following Li et al. (2026); IoT-based data integration across upstream/downstream lines (Li et al., 2024); a simulation model (e.g., the three-stage model, TSM) that computes feasible charging/discharging times respecting L1 constraints before any schedule is evaluated (Li et al., 2026); and parameter-prediction models (LightGBM in Li et al., 2024; GA-BP in Duan et al., 2025) that supply the twin with accurate energy and force estimates.
L3 — AI Decision Layer: two complementary decision engines. (a) Learned policies — DRL (SAC in Wang et al., 2025; PPO/POMDP in Shah et al., 2026) and MARL (Bashyal et al., 2025; Theumer et al., 2022) — handle fast, repetitive scheduling and energy-dispatch decisions. (b) Optimization and metaheuristic solvers — MILP, matheuristics, GA/SA/PSO/GWO (Cluster C1), and robust/chance-constrained models (Cluster C6, e.g., Zhang et al., 2023; Long et al., 2020; Pena et al., 2019) — handle constraint-heavy or highly uncertain sub-problems requiring an exact or robust guarantee. A router selects the engine based on time-criticality and constraint complexity, mirroring how Shah et al. (2026) and Wang et al. (2025) each benchmark DRL directly against MILP rather than treating the two as mutually exclusive.
L4 — Explainability & Governance Layer: XAI methods — SHAP (Theumer et al., 2022), counterfactual explanations (Mehdiyev et al., 2024), decision-tree surrogates (Wang & Chen, 2024) — attach a human-readable rationale to every AI-generated decision before execution. An automation-level router classifies each decision as AI-in-the-loop, Human-in-the-loop, or Human-on-the-loop, following the Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA)-based framework of Arunthavanathan et al. (2024).
L5 — Human & Business Layer: schedulers, furnace/rolling operators, and plant management review XAI-flagged decisions, retain override authority consistent with the human-intervenable marketplace design of Neuer et al. (2016), and set the KPI weighting (energy cost vs. tardiness vs. throughput) that both the digital twin and AI layers optimize against.
Data and control flow: sensor data flows upward from L1 through L2 to L3; recommended decisions flow upward from L3 to L4 for explanation, then to L5 for automation-level-appropriate action (auto-execute, approve, or escalate); approved actions flow back down from L5 to L1 for execution; and outcomes feed back into L2 (twin recalibration) and L3 (policy retraining), closing the loop.

3. Decision-Making & Governance Model
Not all decisions carry the same risk or reversibility. The blueprint assigns each decision type an automation level — AI-in-the-loop (AIiL), Human-in-the-loop (HiL), or Human-on-the-loop (HoL) — following the framework of Arunthavanathan et al. (2024), so that routine, low-stakes decisions are automated while safety-critical or judgment-intensive decisions retain human authority.
4. Respecting Metallurgical & Operational Constraints
The architecture treats the following constraints as binding at L1/L2, independent of which AI method (DRL, MARL, MILP, metaheuristic) generates a candidate decision at L3:
Minimum and maximum heating/residence time per slab or billet (Wang et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2024).
Deterioration effect — processing time increases with a job's waiting time before heating (Xu et al., 2024; Wang, Liu & Jin, 2019).
FIFO ordering and single-operation-at-a-time interlocks within a furnace (charging, stepping, and extracting cannot occur simultaneously) (Li et al., 2026).
Furnace, ladle, and rolling-unit capacity and dimensional limits (Han et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2023).
No-wait / no-idle-machine constraints in continuous-process flow shops (Gomes et al., 2021; Hidri et al., 2021).
Safety Instrumented System (SIS) and Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA) requirements, which mandate a manual shutdown capability that cannot be fully automated (Arunthavanathan et al., 2024).
These constraints are enforced by an independent validation step (Workflow Step 4) rather than being left to the AI decision engine alone, so that a learned policy's recommendation is always checked against the same feasibility rules used by the exact/robust solvers in L3(b).
5. Benefits

6. Risks & Mitigations
Combining Digital Twins, DRL/MARL, optimization, and XAI into a single architecture introduces risks distinct from those of any single method used in isolation. These are addressed explicitly rather than left implicit in the architecture.
7. Deployment Roadmap
The blueprint is deployed incrementally, starting from a single-furnace pilot and progressively extending automation scope and governance maturity, so that trust and validated performance are established before autonomy is increased.
8. Summary Blueprint Statement
This blueprint operationalizes the Document Set's six thematic clusters as a single five-layer system rather than six competing methodologies. Digital Twins supply the accurate, real-time state that makes any downstream decision meaningful; Deep Reinforcement Learning and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning provide fast, autonomous decisions for routine, repetitive scheduling and energy-dispatch problems; classical optimization and robust/uncertainty-aware methods handle constraint-heavy or high-stakes decisions where an exact or provably robust answer is required; Explainable AI ensures every automated recommendation carries a human-interpretable rationale; and an explicit, LOPA-based governance model determines, decision by decision, how much autonomy the system is granted. Metallurgical and safety constraints are enforced independently of which AI method produced a candidate decision, and the phased deployment roadmap ensures that autonomy is extended only as twin accuracy, policy performance, and operator trust are demonstrated at each stage.

Risk | Description | Mitigation
Model–process mismatch | Digital twin or DRL policy trained on historical data may not reflect current furnace/line condition | Continuous twin recalibration and periodic policy retraining via the L1–L3 feedback loop
Over-automation of safety-critical decisions | Removing humans from shutdown or mitigation decisions | Mandatory Human-in-the-loop / AI-in-the-loop classification for safety layers (Arunthavanathan et al., 2024)
Explanation–decision mismatch | An XAI explanation may not faithfully represent the underlying DRL policy's actual reasoning | Use complementary XAI methods (e.g., SHAP and counterfactual) and validate explanation fidelity before deployment (Theumer et al., 2022; Mehdiyev et al., 2024)
Constraint violation by learned policies | A DRL policy may propose actions that violate metallurgical constraints if these are not explicitly encoded | Independent hard-constraint validation layer (action masking / feasibility check) separate from the learned policy (Shah et al., 2026)
Organizational resistance / low adoption | Operators may distrust scheduling decisions perceived as a “black box” | HoL/HiL governance, mandatory XAI explanation, and phased rollout with retained human veto
Integration complexity across sub-systems | Combining digital twins, DRL, optimization, and XAI increases overall system and software complexity | Phased deployment (Section 7), beginning with a single-furnace pilot before scaling
Data and cybersecurity exposure | An IoT-based digital twin depends on continuous, trustworthy sensor data feeds | Standard IT/OT security controls for data integrity and access; flagged as an operational requirement not directly addressed in the reviewed literature
